Question: Is real-time GPS use ("where am I now", walking navigation, turn-by-turn) in scope, or is this purely an exploration/learning tool used at a desk?
Why it matters: Real-time use changes the platform (mobile becomes essential), safety obligations, data freshness needs and the whole UX. Products like Soundscape already occupy that space.
Architect's suggestion / options: Suggest: exploration/learning tool only for v1, with GPS explicitly out of scope. Possibly allow "start at my current location" as a convenience later.
PO Response: This is a desktop exploration tool only.

Question: Is mobile (iOS/Android) a future target, or is desktop (Windows, then Mac) the long-term platform?
Why it matters: Affects technology choice now. Some frameworks give mobile almost for free; others close the door.
Architect's suggestion / options: Options: (a) desktop only; (b) desktop now, mobile later; (c) web app usable on any device.
PO Response: Windows is bare minimum. I would look for Windows and Mac from day one.  Mobile devices is not expected to be a target platform because these will limit the functionality that can be delivered.

Question: Would a browser-based web app be acceptable instead of (or as well as) an installed desktop app?
Why it matters: Web gives the most consistent screen reader behaviour across NVDA, JAWS and VoiceOver, plus built-in HRTF audio. But offline use and large local data are harder in a browser.
Architect's suggestion / options: Suggest: web UI technology wrapped in a desktop shell (e.g. Tauri/Electron) to get both web accessibility and local data storage.
PO Response: I have been pleasantly surprised at how good web apps are now. For example, see the peer folder Sreader which is both a desktop and web app and where the web app is nearly as feature rich as the desktop app.  And in fact, this app provides both a desktop and web version using the same code base.  Maybe this is an option for this project also.

Question: Must the application work fully offline once data is downloaded?
Why it matters: Determines whether we can rely on online services (search, routing, tile servers) or must ship everything locally.
Architect's suggestion / options: Suggest: fully offline after data download, with online used only to fetch data packs.
PO Response: Being online, especially at a desktop, is so common it isn't much of a burden to say you need to be online.  However, performance maybe hindered if you are getting data down purely on demand.  And if you have all the data downloaded, then of course you don't need to be online.  But if the user moves to a new part of the world which is not downloaded and they are not online, well, we can fail gracefully and advise the user.

Question: Is the application intended to be free/open source, commercial, or for a specific organisation?
Why it matters: Affects licensing of dependencies (e.g. GPL vs permissive), data licence compatibility (OSM ODbL share-alike), hosting costs and distribution.
PO Response: I actively do not want anyone to be able to make money directly from this application/tool.  And making it open source and free is great.

Question: Do you have access to blind and partially sighted testers during development? How often could they be involved?
Why it matters: Accessibility UX can't be validated by sighted developers alone. Testing cadence shapes the phased plan.
Architect's suggestion / options: Suggest: a small panel (3-5 users) testing at the end of each phase.
PO Response: The product owner is blind (not partially sighted) and using NVDA on Windows 11.  The PO has access to some other blind friends who maybe willing to help and also to sighted friends.

Question: What level of technical/GIS skill should we assume of the end user? (e.g. comfortable with bearings in degrees? clock-face directions? compass points?)
Why it matters: Determines default output wording and how much configurability is needed.
Architect's suggestion / options: Suggest: configurable direction format (compass points, clock face, degrees) and units (metric/imperial).
PO Response: For bearings I think we will need options e.g. exact degrees, approx degrees, clock face, compass points down to second level.  Position on planet is harder though as I'm not aware of anything simpler than longitude and latitude

Question: Is the primary use case education (e.g. geography lessons), personal curiosity/travel planning, professional (e.g. orientation and mobility trainers), or all of these?
Why it matters: Prioritises features: education favours physical/political geography and quizzes; O&M favours street-level detail.
PO Response: I think it is all of them.  At low zoom levels it is about geography for both education and personal info. At high zoom levels it is the same but also brings in mobility as the tool can help prepare for visiting somewhere ahead of time.

Question: What languages must be supported, both for the UI and for feature names (local name vs English name)?
Why it matters: OSM has multilingual names. Screen readers mispronounce names in the wrong language unless marked up.
Architect's suggestion / options: Suggest: English UI for v1, with user choice of preferred name language and a fall-back to the local name.
PO Response: Agree with the recommendation

Question: Is refreshable Braille a must-have with its own tailored output, or is it enough that the screen reader passes our text to the Braille display?
Why it matters: Tailored Braille output (abbreviated, fixed-position fields) is extra work but much better on 40-cell displays.
Architect's suggestion / options: Suggest: screen reader pass-through for v1, plus a concise "Braille mode" text format.
PO Response: PO is not a Braille user and will need to get feedback from Braille users. But initially go with recommendation.

Question: Do you have a preferred mental model for movement? e.g. (a) hierarchy: zoom in/out of containers; (b) step to neighbouring features; (c) free cursor moving by bearing and distance; (d) following lines.
Why it matters: Core of the UX. My proposal is to offer all four sharing one cursor, but I'd like to know which you see as primary.
Architect's suggestion / options: Suggest: hierarchy and neighbour-stepping as primary for blind users; free cursor for sighted/partially sighted and for exploring open areas like oceans.
PO Response:
I had always thought navigation would be implemented in several ways;
1. Use the cursor keys to move north, east, south and west by a step size and the step size can be varied e.g. 1km, 5km, 25km, 100km, 250km, 1000km.
2. The user can rotate on the spot to face any of north, east, south and west and then move forward by a given step size.
3. The user can rotate by more granular amounts e.g. to 42 degrees. And then move forward.
Methods 2 and 3 allow the user to move over the poles.
For networks;
4. Move from one intersection to another.  The user is at an intersection on the network and can inspect where each link leading from the current node takes them.  e.g. Standing at the junction of Spring Road, Chessel Avenue and West End Road, I can go up Spring Road to the intersection of Spring Road and Catherines Close.
5. Similar to 4, but have the option to stop at POI along the link e.g. A bus stop.
There is still a choice to be made for options 4 and 5 on the orientation of the user.  Do they always face north, or do they face the direction they travel in.
I had never considered a hierarchical model.  Start with the world, which contains continents, which contains countries, which contain ... and so on.
With each layer having options to move to bordering, intersecting or touching neighbours.  But I like this option.
The ability to move around using a mouse is also needed.  As well as the ability to enter in coordinates or do a search and jump to a search result.

Question: When the cursor is in open space (e.g. a field or the middle of an ocean) is it "on" the smallest containing area, or on a point location with the area as context?
Why it matters: Defines what "current focus" means. A point cursor gives precise distances; a feature focus gives simpler navigation.
Architect's suggestion / options: Suggest: two things tracked separately: a cursor position (point) and a focused feature. Queries can use either.
PO Response:
The exact longitude and latitude should always be available to the user.
But when moving around the map, it should say the current position as the smallest polygon under the exact point location. If there is a lake, in a field, which is in a county, and also in a national park, which is in a country, and the user is in the lake, there is a hierarchy of polygons that describe the location and the user should have access to this list but the primary feedback is that they are in the lake.

Question: Which keyboard conventions must we avoid? (e.g. NVDA/JAWS reserve many keys in browse mode; the app will need to run in focus/application mode.)
Why it matters: Keyboard clashes with screen readers are the most common failure in accessible apps.
Architect's suggestion / options: Suggest: a dedicated map region that uses application mode, with all commands re-mappable and a key-help command.
PO Response: Agree.

Question: How verbose should automatic announcements be when moving? e.g. on crossing a border, say "Entering France" automatically, or only on request?
Why it matters: Too much speech is tiring; too little loses context. Needs to be user-configurable but we need a sensible default.
Architect's suggestion / options: Suggest: verbosity levels (terse / normal / detailed) plus per-event toggles.
PO Response: The announcement should announce when something has changed.  So from the response for question 11 , when the user moves off the lake, it tells them they are in a field.  If they move to an adjacent field which also happens to be in a different county, it would announce the name of the new field and the new county.

Question: Should the user be able to ask natural-language questions (e.g. "what rivers flow through Germany?") or is a structured query/menu approach enough?
Why it matters: Natural language needs an LLM or a big grammar and may need to be online. Structured queries are predictable and work offline.
Architect's suggestion / options: Suggest: structured queries for v1 (menus and query commands); consider natural language later as an optional online feature.
PO Response: Natural language queries are a long way down the line and not a priority.  But even structured queries needs to be user friendly and hide  database details.

Question: Should users be able to create their own content: bookmarks, notes, custom routes, or annotations shared with others?
Why it matters: Shared annotations need a backend and user accounts. Local bookmarks are simple.
Architect's suggestion / options: Suggest: local bookmarks and notes in v1; sharing via export/import files.
PO Response: Agree. And by bookmarks I understand you are saying pins or specific locations.  So a user could mark a series of points and ask for the distance between the first and last.  But, and I hadn't thought of this before, the user should also be able to bookmark any feature e.g.  A list of countries.

Question: Is measuring route distance (along roads/paths) needed, or is straight-line distance enough?
Why it matters: Route distance needs a routing engine and network graph per region: significant extra data and processing.
Architect's suggestion / options: Suggest: straight-line for v1; network distance along a single followed line; full routing later if needed.
PO Response: Distance along a route is needed, but not based on a shortest-distance algorithm.  It would only be for a linear route which is unambiguous.

Question: What headphones/audio setup can we assume? HRTF only works well with stereo headphones.
Why it matters: Determines whether HRTF is a default or an option, and the fallback for speakers.
Architect's suggestion / options: Suggest: HRTF with headphones as default, simple stereo panning plus pitch for speakers.
PO Response: This is an option the user can select with default being HRTF/headphones

Question: Should spatial sound use the map's orientation (north = ahead) or the user's chosen heading (rotate to face a direction)?
Why it matters: Affects how bearings are heard. A fixed north is easier to learn; a rotatable heading suits "looking around".
Architect's suggestion / options: Suggest: north-up by default with an optional "face direction" heading.
PO Response: This is related to question 11.  The answer to how HRTF behaves depends on the navigation method.

Question: For grid/z-value layers (e.g. rainfall), is sonifying values as pitch while moving the cursor the expected approach? Any other ideas you had in mind?
Why it matters: Confirms the scope of data sonification beyond distance/bearing.
Architect's suggestion / options: Suggest: pitch for value, plus a "sweep" command that plays a row or region of values as a sequence.
PO Response:
Yes, pitch is the primary indicator.
But sweeping is a good idea.  The user could ask for a sweep from left to right, or top to bottom, between a range.
Also related to question 11 as the sweep should reflect the current navigation mode.

Question: What touch devices are expected: touchscreen laptops/Surface tablets, Windows touch monitors, iPads, or graphics tablets?
Why it matters: Touch exploration on a desktop OS behaves very differently from a tablet, and screen readers intercept touch gestures.
Architect's suggestion / options: Suggest: treat touch as a later phase; design for Windows touchscreens and trackpad/graphics tablet with absolute positioning.
PO Response:
My main reason for including touch devices is that it provides a mechanism for a blind user to get tactile feedback about the map rather than as an alternative input mechanism for controlling the application.
For example, one feature could be to display a country (or any polygon) in isolation on the screen.  Then when a finger is placed inside the polygon, a high pitched sound is made.  If the finger moves outside the polygon, it changes to a low pitch sound. The user can use the audio feedback to trace the outline of the polygon.  
I could come up with other examples where the sound generated by the location of the finger on the screen can be used to give a sense of physicalness to the data.
I suspect we develop these on a case-by-case basis but I don't want to leave this sort of thing to last.

Question: For partially sighted users, beyond high contrast and isolating features, are there specific needs? e.g. magnification support, large text labels, colour-blind safe palettes, simplified styling.
Why it matters: Determines the visual styling work and whether we need our own map renderer or can style an existing one.
Architect's suggestion / options: Suggest: several built-in themes (high contrast dark/light, colour-blind safe) plus per-layer show/hide and label size.
PO Response:
Magnification and large labels should be left to the typical zoom feature of a map, or to the user's dedicated magnification software.
Colour-blind safe or high-contrast colour palettes is sensible.
I don't know what you mean by simplified styling.

Question: Should sighted and blind users be able to work together in real time (e.g. both see the same cursor on a shared screen, or across two computers)?
Why it matters: Same-screen is simple (shared focus). Across two computers needs networking and is a big extra.
Architect's suggestion / options: Suggest: same screen only for v1, with the visual map always showing the non-visual cursor and focus.
PO Response: Work together only means sitting at the same computer. I don't mean screen sharing or sharing data other than what goes to a centralised database.

Question: What level of detail is required worldwide versus in selected regions? e.g. is street-level detail needed for the whole world, or only for regions a user downloads?
Why it matters: Full-planet OSM is ~80GB compressed and several hundred GB processed. This drives the whole data architecture.
Architect's suggestion / options: Suggest: worldwide base pack (countries, seas, major physical features, major rivers/roads/cities) plus downloadable regional detail packs.
PO Response: Agree with recommendation

Question: Is there a target region for the first release (e.g. UK) we can use to prove the detailed street-level tier?
Why it matters: Lets us build and test the full pipeline on manageable data before scaling.
Architect's suggestion / options: Suggest: one country (e.g. the UK) for street-level detail in the early phases.
PO Response: We can use the UK as an example during development, but at any time we should be able to switch to a different part of the world.  Relevant for regression testing and making sure the map is generic for worldwide coverage.

Question: How often must data be updated? One-off, yearly, monthly?
Why it matters: Determines whether the data pipeline needs to be automated and repeatable, and whether incremental updates are needed.
Architect's suggestion / options: Suggest: fully scripted, repeatable pipeline; release refreshed packs a few times a year; no incremental updates in v1.
PO Response:
Ideally map data is refreshed automatically or on regular schedules.
Having said that, a lot of data does not change rapidly.  So the answer is probably dependent on each dataset.

Question: Who will host the data packs for download, and is there a budget for hosting/bandwidth?
Why it matters: Packs of hundreds of MB to several GB need hosting (e.g. GitHub Releases, cloud storage, a CDN).
PO Response: I don't know the answer to this.  All I can say is that there is no budget.

Question: How should disputed borders and territories be presented? (e.g. Kashmir, Crimea, Western Sahara)
Why it matters: Political neutrality and data source choice. Natural Earth offers several "points of view"; OSM follows on-the-ground control.
Architect's suggestion / options: Suggest: state the source's view and mark disputed areas as disputed in announcements.
PO Response: Data source dependent and have to go with the policy of the data source.

Question: For maritime boundaries, do you want both views available: land-only country shapes AND territorial waters / EEZ as separate layers?
Why it matters: Resolves the OSM land/sea boundary issue you raised. Clipping to coastlines is a standard approach.
Architect's suggestion / options: Suggest: land-clipped countries by default; maritime zones (territorial sea, EEZ from Marine Regions) as optional layers.
PO Response: The primary aim is to show coastlines accurately.  However, territorial waters is an interesting political dataset that would be interesting to be able to provide but is not core.

Question: Are you aware of any licence restrictions on the IHO and other specialist sources you intend to use? e.g. IHO S-23 and Marine Regions data have specific (sometimes non-commercial) terms.
Why it matters: Data must be free and attributable. Some sources restrict commercial use or redistribution.
Architect's suggestion / options: I'll research licences for each candidate source as part of the design, but any known constraints help.
PO Response: I will be looking to you to research data sources.  As far as I know though, IHO does provide useful data we can make use of under free to use licensing.

Question: Which grid/z-value datasets did you have in mind (e.g. rainfall, temperature, population density, elevation)?
Why it matters: Each needs a source, a resolution and a storage approach (raster tiles).
Architect's suggestion / options: Suggest: start with one: elevation or rainfall from a free global source (e.g. WorldClim, Copernicus DEM).
PO Response:
I actually don't have a strong idea in this area.  It isn't an area I've looked at much.  But elevation, depth, precipitation and temperature are all good starting points.
I'd also add tthat I do want data about features.  Areas, population of habitations,  links to wikipedia are examples.

Question: What does the data manager actually do in the tool? e.g. run the pipeline, choose regions/layers, fix or merge data, review quality, publish packs?
Why it matters: Defines whether this is a simple scripted pipeline with a front end or a full editing application.
Architect's suggestion / options: Suggest: v1 is a scripted, configuration-driven pipeline with an accessible command-line/simple UI; no manual geometry editing.
PO Response: Agree with recommendation especially since the data manager could also be blind and manually editting geometries is not an option.

Question: Are the data managers also screen reader users? Are they technical (comfortable with command line, config files)?
Why it matters: Determines how much UI the data tool needs.
PO Response: Assume the data manager is technical both in terms of mapping knowledge and computer usage

Question: Should end users be able to build their own custom packs (e.g. pick a region and layers) or only download pre-built ones?
Why it matters: Custom packs need either a server-side builder or shipping the pipeline to users.
Architect's suggestion / options: Suggest: pre-built packs only in v1.
PO Response: Pre-built packs only for all versions.

Question: What development resources exist besides Claude Code? Is there a human developer to review, test and deploy?
Why it matters: Shapes how the implementation plan is written (level of detail, review gates, manual steps).
PO Response: No human developer.  Development will be a case of requirement specification, approved development plan, phased implementation base on dev/test cycles carried out by Claude/product owner

Question: Are there any technology preferences or constraints? e.g. languages you or your team know, existing code to reuse, hosting already available.
Why it matters: Avoids recommending a stack nobody can maintain.
PO Response:
I do have an example implementation for both data collection and the desktop application I can show you which I wrote in C++ using Qt.  However, I don't want to show you this until you've done a high level design as I don't want to steer you down any particular route.
Having said that, with the advent of agentic code development, and as I have had success with this in other projects, I would be happy for Python to be the main language as as a product owner I should not need to look at it.
There are no other human resources on the project currently or expected to be.
If another language or platform provides advantages then I am happy for this to drive the solution.

Question: Is there a target timeline or a point at which a first usable version is needed (e.g. for a demo or user trial)?
Why it matters: Determines the scope of phase 1 / MVP.
PO Response: There are no time constraints.

Question: Should the project be set up as a git repository (e.g. on GitHub) from the start?
Why it matters: Needed for Claude Code phased development, CI testing and releases. The folder is not currently a git repo.
Architect's suggestion / options: Suggest: yes, a GitHub repository with CI for automated tests and release builds.
PO Response: Yes, GitHub.

Question: When providing directional information through sound icons, should speech notifications support this by matching the direction and volume of the sound icon?
Why it matters: Determines what TTS engines are used
PO Response: As an end user, if a sound is made indicating a particular direction and distance, it would be great if the spoken label e.g. Berlin, also came from the same direction.

Question: You said you do not want anyone to make money directly from the tool, and that open source is great. Open source licences (OSI definition) cannot forbid commercial use, and the OSM data licence (ODbL) explicitly allows commercial use of our data packs. Which matters more: being formally open source, or blocking commercial use?
Why it matters: Determines the code licence and how we describe the project. The data side cannot be made non-commercial while it uses OSM.
Architect's suggestion / options: Options: (a) GPL-3.0 or AGPL-3.0: genuinely open source; anyone selling a modified version must publish their source, which removes most of the profit motive. (b) A non-commercial source-available licence such as PolyForm Noncommercial: forbids selling, but is not 'open source' and some contributors and distributors avoid it. Recommendation: (a) GPL-3.0, and accept that the data stays ODbL.
PO Response: OSM is such a valuable source we can't exclude it.  So GPL3 will be fine.

Question: In network (junction to junction) and line-following modes, should the user face the direction of travel or stay facing north? (Follow-up to DP11 and DP19.)
Why it matters: Changes how links are described (left/right versus compass) and where sounds appear.
Architect's suggestion / options: Recommendation: face the direction of travel by default. Links are described relative to the user first, then by compass, e.g. 'Ahead slightly left, Spring Road, north-east, 140 m'. A setting keeps north-up for those who prefer it.
PO Response:
The answer depends on the navigation mode.
See answer to question 11.
There is a navigation mode where the user always faces north.  In this case, when navigating a network, the options for links are described as absolute  values relative to north.  The units are another option e.g. degrees, compass or clock face.
If the user is in "free roaming"  navigation mode where they can orientate themselves to any bearing, then navigation through a network then options for links are relative to current direction of travel.
For the navigation snapping to NESW, treat the bearings as relative to the current face forward direction.
Note we'll want a keystroke to allow the user to cycle through the 3 navigation modes.

Question: In compass mode (arrow keys = N/E/S/W), what should happen at the poles, where 'east' and 'north' stop making sense?
Why it matters: Avoids confusing behaviour at the edge of the world.
Architect's suggestion / options: Recommendation: stop at the pole with the message 'North Pole. Use heading mode to continue over the pole.' Alternative: switch automatically into heading mode.
PO Response: If by moving north or south the next move takes the user over the pole, play a blocking sound.  I'll provide a wav file for this sound.  And the user remains unmoved.

Question: When a step changes nothing (e.g. 100 km steps across mid-ocean), should anything be spoken?
Why it matters: Silence can feel like a missed key press; repeating the same name is tiring.
Architect's suggestion / options: Recommendation: a soft 'tick' earcon only. Space confirms where you are. Verbosity 'detailed' repeats the area name.
PO Response: Agree with recommendation.  If needed, I can provide a wav file for the soft tick sound.

Question: Should line features crossed during a step (rivers, roads, railways, borders) be announced automatically?
Why it matters: Without it, large steps silently jump over important features. With it, city-level steps could list many roads.
Architect's suggestion / options: Recommendation: on by default for rivers, railways and major roads, with per-category toggles. If more than 3 are crossed, say 'crossed 7 lines' and offer a command to list them.
PO Response:
I was initially planning to just not announce anything when taking a step that jumps over features.
I was going to want a "what's nearby" list the user can navigate.  In fact, I still do.
But having a list of "Crossed features" is a good idea. It should be silent though. 
Jumping a polygon or a line is a very clear concept.
I also want to know if the user came close to a point feature e.g. They passed within 1km of a railway station.  I accept this could be a complex calculation and so might not be practical.
The distance for this "passed nearby" value should be changeable by the user.
It will also be affected by the current step size since large steps will skip many features.

Question: In compass and heading modes, when should point features (bus stops, bins, crossings) be mentioned, given they rarely sit exactly under the cursor?
Why it matters: Points are only reachable by query unless we define a 'near' rule.
Architect's suggestion / options: Recommendation: never automatically by default. Option: a proximity sound (soft ping from its direction) when a point of a chosen category is within half a step. 'R' lists them.
PO Response:
See response to question 44.
We are going to need a way to detect nearby points since, as you say, it will be near impossible to land on one exactly.

Question: Spatialised spoken labels (DP39) must use a voice built into the app, not your screen reader's voice. Is that acceptable? And should the same text also go to NVDA (spoken twice) or only to Braille/history?
Why it matters: A screen reader's voice cannot be positioned in 3D space; we have to generate the speech ourselves. You have an eSpeakPlus project. Is there a voice or engine you prefer?
Architect's suggestion / options: Recommendation: Windows/macOS system voices rendered to audio on desktop, eSpeak NG in the web version. Screen reader copy goes to the history and Braille only, by default.
PO Response: I agree that the screen reader voice cannot be sent through HRTF or even panning.  So we need our own TTS.  How you make this pass through a positioning algorithm is up to you as the software engineer.

Question: Would you (and possibly friends) take part in an early listening test of spatial sound (direction and front/back accuracy with HRTF), before the rest of the sound design is built on it?
Why it matters: HRTF front/back confusion is common and varies between people. Better to find out in week one than at the end.
Architect's suggestion / options: Recommendation: a small standalone test page in Phase 1, recording how accurately you judge directions.
PO Response: As the PO I will be the tester for this early work.

Question: Hosting with no budget: are you happy for the data packs to be published as GitHub Releases on the project repository (free, no bandwidth limit, each file under 2 GiB)?
Why it matters: Without hosting, there are no downloads. Other free options need extra accounts.
Architect's suggestion / options: Recommendation: GitHub Releases. Fall-back: Cloudflare R2 free tier (needs a card on file) or Hugging Face datasets.
PO Response: Let's start with GitHub.  Only if widespread user demand needs it will we look at other options.

Question: Desktop and web from one code base: should the first usable release be desktop (Windows + Mac) with the web following, or both together? Is it acceptable if the web version has fewer features (e.g. smaller offline data, no touch tracing)?
Why it matters: The browser limits local storage size and some audio/TTS options. Doing both at once slows the first release.
Architect's suggestion / options: Recommendation: design the core so it runs in both from day one, release desktop first, and release web one phase later.
PO Response:
As the PO, I only have access to a Windows 11 laptop.
I have had no success in the past in getting help from a blind Mac user so all we can do is make design decisions that are inline with the desktop being deployable to Mac but we will not necessarily get real user feedback for a long time.
By doing a web version in parallel with a Windows desktop we can attract a larger number of users and stimulate interest in the application.  This will increase the chances of getting a Mac user to do desktop testing.

Question: What is the maximum size you would accept for the worldwide base pack that everyone must download? And how should regional packs be cut: by country, or by smaller regions for big countries (e.g. US states, English regions)?
Why it matters: Sets the level of detail in the base pack and the pack catalogue structure.
Architect's suggestion / options: Recommendation: base pack 1 GB or less. Regional packs follow Geofabrik's extract boundaries (country, split into sub-regions for large countries), since that matches our source.
PO Response:
Let us set an initial limit of 250Mb for a base pack and see where this gets us.  If this is too limiting, that is the amount of interesting data is too small or coarse, then we can review this soft limit.
Other packs I think will be data driven but 1Gb is probably an upper limit.   But this is not a hard rule.

Question: Facts such as population and area will come from Wikidata, a crowd-sourced database. It is usually good but occasionally wrong or out of date. Is that acceptable, with the source and date shown in details?
Why it matters: Trust in the figures we speak.
Architect's suggestion / options: Recommendation: yes. Show 'Population 67 million (Wikidata, 2024)'.
PO Response: Wikipedia /wikidata are okay data sources.  If practical, we can have a placwe where we list the sources of data.

Question: Hierarchy mode: a lake can be in a field, a county and a national park at once, and a sea can be in an ocean. When the user presses 'up', which parent should it go to?
Why it matters: Without a rule, 'up' is unpredictable.
Architect's suggestion / options: Recommendation: 'lenses' the user switches between. Political (default): area > county > region > country > continent. Physical/marine: bay > sea > ocean, or range > system. Designations: national parks etc. The containment list always shows every parent.
PO Response:
It is only ambiguous if the next level up is not fully contained within the next polygon above that.  
In this situation, make a small beep, display a popup menu listing the two options. The user can then select which to go to.

Question: Building data packs from OSM needs a reasonably powerful machine (the free GitHub build servers have too little disk for anything bigger than a small country). What computer will the pipeline run on: your own PC? How much RAM and free disk space does it have?
Why it matters: Decides whether pack building is local or in the cloud, and how big the regions can be.
Architect's suggestion / options: Recommendation: build on your PC. Each country build is a scripted, unattended run. Free CI only runs the tests and small sample builds.
PO Response:
My laptop has a 1Tb SSD C: drive but it is currently 80% full so can only be used for small dataset manipulation.

Question: In DP41 you asked for one key to cycle 'the 3 navigation modes'. Architect's suggestion / options: Recommendation: yes, as described in section 4 of the UX description and NAV-12. Each orientation works with every movement mode. For example, network mode in north-fixed describes roads by compass direction, and in free facing describes them relative to the direction of travel.
PO Response: See UXReview.txt.

Question: Cardinal facing (snap to N/E/S/W) needs two rules. (a) Facing east or west and stepping forward: follow the line of latitude (like the arrow keys in north-fixed), or follow a great circle, which slowly drifts away from due east? (b) In network or line mode, after travelling along a road that bends, which way does the user face on arrival?
Why it matters: You said bearings in this mode are relative to the way the user faces, so we need to know which way that is after every move.
Architect's suggestion / options: Recommendation: (a) follow the line of latitude when facing east or west; facing north or south, carry on over the pole and come out facing the other way. (b) On arrival, face whichever of N, E, S or W is closest to the direction of travel, and announce it only if it changed, e.g. 'Now facing east'.
PO Response: See UXReview.txt.

Question: The crossed and passed list (Shift+X) is silent, as you asked. Question: Hierarchy 'up' beeps and shows a menu when two parents overlap without one containing the other. In the UK, many boundary types overlap: counties, national parks, civil parishes, electoral wards, postcode areas, police areas and so on. Which categories should take part in the hierarchy?

Question: Your review asked for one way of moving, and for search to only jump. Version 0.2 also had a 'focus': a feature you could ask about without moving there. Shall I drop focus altogether? The current feature would then always be what you are on: the smallest area when stepping, the feature you moved to in hierarchy mode, or the junction in network mode.
Why it matters: Focus was a second thing to keep track of, and you did not ask for it. Without it, the model is simpler: you are somewhere, and everything is about where you are.
Architect's suggestion / options: Recommendation: drop focus. To learn about something else without going there, select it in the Information panel and choose details, or its own Bordering, Contains and so on. See section 1 and 6.3 of the UX description and LOC-4.
PO Response: Yes, drop focus.

Question: You said information should be grouped by things like bordering, nearby and contains. I propose an Information panel: a tree whose top level is Within, Contains, Bordering, Overlapping, Crossing, Nearby, Crossed and passed, and Search. A key in the map opens each group (Shift+Space, I, N, O, X, R, Shift+X). Is this what you meant? Are any groups missing or unnecessary?
Why it matters: This replaces the 'Results list' that confused you in version 0.2. It is the main way information reaches the user, so it needs to match your mental model.
Architect's suggestion / options: Recommendation: as described in section 6 of the UX description and INF-10. Groups are only worked out when opened, so they never slow down movement.
PO Response: Accept recommendation.  However, will give feedback during development and is an area which is likely to change based on testing/experience.

Question: You asked about zooming. I propose one 'scale' control (Page Up and Page Down) that sets the step size, the map zoom (about 20 steps across the screen), the range of sounds, the Nearby radius and the level of detail announced. A sighted user zooming with the mouse wheel changes the scale too. Should the scale and the map zoom always be locked together, or adjustable separately?
Why it matters: If they are separate, a blind user and a sighted helper can end up at different scales without knowing it, and the sound range no longer matches what is visible.
Architect's suggestion / options: Recommendation: always locked together. One control, one idea of scale, shared by everyone. See section 4 of the UX description and NAV-13.
PO Response: Step and zoom need to be independent of each other, although it is an option for the user to have them linked.  The behaviours you detailed are linked to zoom and not step.  Having them separate allows the user to move in small increments whilst receiving information at the same level of detail.  It also mimics the sighted users use of a mouse since they can click either only a small or a large distance from the centre to move.

Question: At a large scale, hearing 'Field' after a 25 km step is useless. I propose that an area is only announced automatically if its width is at least a quarter of the step size, and that each line and point layer has a range of scales at which it appears in the crossed and passed list. Small areas are still listed by Space and Shift+Space. Is this rule sensible, and should the user be able to change the quarter-step factor?
Why it matters: Without a rule like this, large steps produce useless announcements and the crossed and passed list fills with minor roads.
Architect's suggestion / options: Recommendation: yes, with the factor adjustable in settings. See section 4.2 of the UX description and ANN-7.
PO Response: I don't follow your assertion that saying field after a 25km step is useless.  If you are in a field, then say you are in a field.  Perhaps I am misunderstanding you.

Question: You said scaling distance into sound defeated a previous project. I propose that distance is always heard relative to the scale: the hearing range is 10 steps, loudness falls with the logarithm of distance (each doubling of distance is about equally quieter), and anything beyond the range plays at the quietest level and sounds muffled. Do you want to try this in the Phase 1 listening test before it is agreed?
Why it matters: A fixed scale cannot suit both a street and a continent. Tying distance to the scale means the same cue always means 'near' or 'far' compared with what you are looking at.
Architect's suggestion / options: Recommendation: yes, and include distance judgements in the Phase 1 listening test alongside direction. Range and curve are settings, so they can be tuned. See section 8.3 of the UX description and SON-9.
PO Response: Yes, link to scale/zoom.  Need to handle the window being different sizes although would normally expect the application to be maximized.  And note earlier answer that zoom/scale are different to step.

Question: Now that lines are just simple networks, going round an island's coastline with no junctions would go all the way round in one move. I propose that travel along a link stops at whichever comes first: the next junction, the next stop point (if switched on), or the step distance. Is that acceptable?
Why it matters: Without a limit, links with no junctions, such as a coastline or a long river reach, cannot be explored in parts.
Architect's suggestion / options: Recommendation: yes. At a large scale this behaves as junction to junction. At a small scale it becomes a walk along the line. Pressing 3 again cycles the network type: roads, roads and paths, railways, waterways, coastline, borders. See section 5.5 and NAV-5.
PO Response: I accept recommendation.

Question: Two parts. (a) In network mode, Left and Right choose links, so turning needs other keys. I propose Shift+Left and Shift+Right to turn 90 degrees, and Ctrl+Left and Ctrl+Right for the fine turn, in every movement mode. In stepping mode, plain Left and Right also turn, as before. Are these acceptable? (b) Your review did not answer DP57 part (a): in cardinal facing, facing east or west, should a step follow the line of latitude (staying at the same latitude), or a great circle (which slowly drifts away from due east)?
Why it matters: You asked for a way to change orientation in cardinal facing after arriving at a junction. Part (b) decides what 'east' means when moving.
Architect's suggestion / options: Recommendation: (a) yes. (b) follow the line of latitude, like north-fixed, so that 'east' always means due east. See sections 5.2 and 5.3 and NAV-12.
PO Response: Yes, those keystrokes are fine. And in cardinal mode, follow the line of latitude for east and west travel.

Question: Contains lists, such as the 2,570 railway stations in the UK, can be very long. Two parts. (a) Should long lists be sorted by name with type-ahead (typing 'Wo' jumps to Woking), plus a command to regroup them by county or the next administrative level down? (b) A feature only partly inside an area, such as the New Forest National Park within Hampshire: should it be listed under Hampshire marked 'partly', or left out?
Why it matters: Long flat lists are slow to use with a screen reader. Leaving out partly-inside features hides real information; including them without a mark is misleading.
Architect's suggestion / options: Recommendation: (a) yes to both. (b) list it, marked 'partly'. See section 5.4 and INF-4.
PO Response:
Using the train station example, only return stations that are visible on the map.   The user should be able to sort by name, distance and bearing.
And a feature only partly inside is still counted.  No need to say partial.  But just as long as it is visible.

Question: Your DP62 answer said the parent must be larger than the current polygon. That happens when two areas share exactly the same boundary, such as the Isle of Wight as a ceremonial county and a unitary authority. Question: About your three new feature ideas. (a) Orientation beacon: should it be able to point at any pin, such as 'home', as well as the North Pole? Question: Projection: I agree with your 'view from space' idea, which is called orthographic projection, centred on your location. Non-visual features never use a projection, because all distances and bearings are calculated on the globe. A small challenge: you said no marker is needed at the centre. I agree for the location itself, since the map is always centred. But a sighted helper may still find it hard to see the exact point being described. May I add a small centre cross that can be switched off?
Why it matters: The projection affects only the visual map and touch tracing. The centre cross helps the blind user and a sighted helper talk about the same exact point.
Architect's suggestion / options: Recommendation: orthographic projection, north-up by default, with an option for heading-up. A small centre cross, on by default and switchable. See section 11 and VIS-1 and VIS-5.
PO Response: Agreed. Please make the cross a plus shape rather than an x shape.

Question: You suggested that crossing lines of latitude and longitude, the prime meridian and the antimeridian might be handled by a data layer. I agree. I propose a 'graticule and special lines' layer: lines of latitude and longitude at an interval you choose (calculated, so no data needed), plus the equator, tropics, polar circles and international date line from Natural Earth. Like any line layer, it can be shown, listed when crossed, followed in network mode, and given a crossing earcon. Is that acceptable?

Question: You said the hearing range follows the zoom, and the application must cope with different window sizes (DP67). I propose that the zoom is a distance: 'Zoom 5 kilometres' means everything within 5 km of the location is in view, measured from the centre to the nearer edge of the map. Resizing the window then only changes how large things are drawn. The same area of the world stays in view and in hearing range. Is that acceptable?
Why it matters: The alternative is a fixed drawing scale, where a smaller window shows less of the world. Then shrinking the window would make features go silent, and the blind user would not know why. A sighted user with a small window would see things drawn smaller rather than see less.
Architect's suggestion / options: Recommendation: zoom is a distance (the view radius), so the window size never changes what is heard, what is listed, or what counts as visible. See section 4.1 of the UX description, NAV-13 and SON-9.
PO Response: I think we have no choice to go with zoom is a distance otherwise the UX will be awful.

Question: Lists such as Contains now show only what is visible (DP70). That makes the zoom matter in hierarchy mode. Going up to the United Kingdom while zoomed in to 1 km, then pressing Down, would list only what is within 1 km. I propose that moving to a feature in hierarchy mode zooms the view to fit it ('United Kingdom. Zoom 1000 kilometres'), and moving down to a smaller feature zooms back in. Jumping to an area from search or the Information panel would do the same. Jumping to a point or coordinates would keep the zoom. Going back with Backspace restores the old zoom. The step size never changes, unless it is linked to the zoom. Is that acceptable?
Why it matters: Without this, hierarchy mode would only work if the user remembered to zoom out first. With it, the sighted helper also sees the whole feature, which matches what a sighted map user expects when choosing a place.
Architect's suggestion / options: Recommendation: yes, zoom to fit in hierarchy mode and when jumping to an area. Stepping, network mode and driving never change the zoom. See sections 5.4 and 5.7 of the UX description, NAV-4 and NAV-8.
PO Response: I accept this recommendation

Question: You said Contains should list only what is visible on the map (DP70). Two parts. (a) Should the same apply to Nearby, look around, and Crossed and passed? (b) I propose that Within, Bordering, Overlapping, Crossing and Search are not limited by zoom, because they are about the current feature's own relationships or about what you asked for. Question: Keys and default lists for zoom and step. I propose: Page Up and Page Down zoom out and in. Shift+Page Up and Shift+Page Down make the step larger and smaller. Ctrl+Page Up and Ctrl+Page Down stay as driving speed. Ctrl+S in the Information panel cycles the sort order (name, distance, bearing). 'Link step to zoom' is off by default and is in the menu and settings, with no key. When linked, the step is one tenth of the zoom distance. Zooms run from 100 m to 10,000 km (the whole hemisphere), and steps from 10 m to 1000 km. Are these acceptable?

Question:
This is DP78 asked again more simply. The question: when you zoom in close, should a list shrink to what is in view, or keep showing everything?

The lists fall into two kinds.

Kind 1, lists that gather many features in an area: Contains, Nearby, look around, and Crossed and passed. These can be huge. The UK has 2,570 railway stations and tens of thousands of bus stops. You already said Contains shows only what is visible. Should the other three do the same? Examples:
- Nearby, zoomed in to 1 km in Southampton: bus stops, shops and streets within 1 km. Zoomed out to 250 km: towns, cities and motorways within 250 km, but no bus stops.
- Crossed and passed, after a 25 km step while zoomed out to 250 km: the motorway and the river you crossed, but not the 40 lanes.

Kind 2, lists about one feature's own relationships, or about something you asked for: Within, Bordering, Overlapping, Crossing and Search. These are short anyway. If they were limited to what is in view, they would often be empty:
- Zoomed in to a street in Paris, Bordering for France would list nothing, because Spain, Germany and the rest are hundreds of kilometres away and out of view.
- Searching for Tokyo while zoomed in on Paris would find nothing, because Tokyo is out of view.
So I suggest these always show everything.

In both kinds, a layer you have switched off is always left out.
Why it matters: Kind 1 lists need a limit, or they become too long to use with a screen reader. Kind 2 lists would look broken if they were limited.
Architect's suggestion / options: Recommendation: limit Kind 1 lists (Contains, Nearby, look around, Crossed and passed) to what is visible at the current zoom. Kind 2 lists (Within, Bordering, Overlapping, Crossing, Search) always show everything from the layers that are switched on. 'Where am I' is never limited, as you said in DP66.
PO Response:
Kind 1, lists that gather many features in an area: Contains, Nearby, look around, and Crossed and passed. 
> I imagine being at the UK level and expanding all bus stops will grind the application to a halt and not be that useful to the user.
> So perhaps we have a zoom level range for point collections just like we will for the size of polygons 
> and yes, these then get applied to nearby,  look around, crossed and passed 

Kind 2, lists about one feature's own relationships, or about something you asked for: Within, Bordering, Overlapping, Crossing and Search. These are short anyway. If they were limited to what is in view, they would often be empty:
> Agreed, but it may lead to confusing sonification experience.
> e.g. How loud to play the HRTF sound for a bordering country not visible on the map?

Question:
Unnamed islands. The UK alone has thousands of islands, and many have no name in OpenStreetMap. Every island is part of the land, so standing on one you would hear its county and country. Should unnamed islands above a minimum size also be announced as 'unnamed island', and counted in Contains?

Why it matters: Without it, a user cannot tell they are on a small island rather than the mainland, unless they explore the coast. With it, Contains lists may fill with unnamed islands.
Architect's suggestion / options: Recommendation: yes, for unnamed islands of 1 hectare (100 m by 100 m) or more, with the size set in configuration. Smaller ones are just land. They are not listed by name in Search. Spike S2 will report how many there are in the UK at each size, so the threshold can be adjusted.
PO Response:
I don't really understand what you are suggesting as the difference in behaviour between above and below  1 hectare.  But an unamed island should be called "Unnamed island".  This means lots of bits of land will be called "Unnamed island".    
At high enough zoom level, all islands should be visible no matter how small they are.
We may have to do some tuning if performance is poor to ensure the zoom level at which certain areas become rendered is suitable.

Question: Continents for distant parts of a country. Some countries have parts on another continent: Spain has the Canary Islands, Ceuta and Melilla in Africa; the USA has Hawaii in the Pacific. (French Guiana would be its own entry, so it is simply in South America.) Should each part be placed in the continent it is physically on, so Spain appears in both Europe and Africa, as Russia appears in both Europe and Asia (DAT-12)?
Why it matters: It decides what 'where am I' says in Tenerife or Ceuta, and what Contains lists for Africa.
Architect's suggestion / options: Recommendation: yes. Each part goes in the continent it is on. In Tenerife you would hear 'Tenerife, Canary Islands, Spain, Africa'. Spain is listed in Contains for both Europe and Africa.
PO Response: Recommendation agreed

Question:
Where the base pack's countries come from. The plan uses Natural Earth for the worldwide base pack, and OpenStreetMap for regional packs. An alternative is to build the base pack's countries and first-level divisions from OpenStreetMap too, cut to the coast and simplified, using the same method spike S2 tests on the UK, France and Spain.

Should the base pack use OpenStreetMap for countries and first-level divisions, if spike S2 shows they fit the 250 MB budget?
Why it matters: OpenStreetMap gives the same coastline, names and identifiers at every zoom, so nothing jumps when a regional pack takes over. Natural Earth is smaller, already cleaned, and has views for disputed areas.
Architect's suggestion / options: Recommendation: yes, if S2 shows it fits and builds reliably. Natural Earth would still provide disputed-area views and a fall-back for any country that fails to build. I will bring the S2 measurements back before this is final.
PO Response: Accept recommendation

Question: Spike S6 compares voices for the spatial labels: eSpeak NG, Piper, and the voices already installed in Windows (the ones NVDA can use). A Windows voice can be placed in space on the desktop, but it cannot be used in the web version, where the choice is eSpeak NG or Piper. If you prefer a Windows voice, is it acceptable for the desktop and web versions to use different voices?
Why it matters: It decides whether the Windows voices are worth including in the spike.
Architect's suggestion / options: Recommendation: yes, it is acceptable, and the difference is listed in Help. The desktop could also offer a choice of voice, with eSpeak NG as the default.
PO Response: No, do not use Windows voices

Question: AtMap used the Synthizer library for spatial sound with HRTF. What was your experience? In particular: could you tell left from right and front from back, did distance sound right, and were there any problems with it, such as delays, clicks or installation?
Why it matters: Synthizer is one of the candidates in spike S1. Your experience is better evidence than anything I can read.
Architect's suggestion / options: No recommendation. Any impressions help, even brief ones.
PO Response: There were no issues with synthizer and I would like to do side-by-side comparisons of it with other HRTF models.

Question: You said the installer is Windows only at first. I plan to keep the automatic tests running on macOS for every change, which costs nothing and stops Windows-only code creeping in (PLT-2), but not to produce Mac downloads until a Mac tester is found. Is that acceptable?
Why it matters: Producing Mac downloads takes extra work on every release, and nobody can test them yet.
Architect's suggestion / options: Recommendation: yes, as described.
PO Response: Recommendation accepted

Question: In spike S5, Tab moves round four regions: the map, the Information panel, Details and the menu bar. When Tab reaches the menu bar, the Map menu opens, in both the desktop and web versions, and Tab again closes it and goes back to the map. Alt also opens the menu bar on the desktop. Does this feel right with NVDA, or would you rather Tab cycled only the first three regions, with the menu bar reached by Alt alone?
Why it matters: UX section 2 makes the menu bar the fourth Tab stop. A menu bar cannot take focus without opening a menu in Qt, so the web version was made to match.
Architect's suggestion / options: Recommendation: keep it as built, unless it feels odd in use. Please try both versions and say.
PO Response: Tabbing should only go to the main regions, not the menu.  In desktop, alt will activate the menu. For web, I think we need a keyboard shortcut, maybe control+alt+M, to take the user to the first top level menu item i.e. Map, but not to open it.

Question: Both Firefox and Chrome now have ariaNotify, the new way for a web page to send speech to the screen reader. The web version uses it, and falls back to live regions in older browsers. Adding ?announcer=live to the end of the web address forces the older live regions. Could you try both with NVDA in Firefox and Chrome, and say whether either is missing, late or cut off when you hold an arrow key?
Why it matters: NVDA's support for ariaNotify in Firefox is new, and I cannot hear the difference myself. Architecture 4.4 assumed Firefox would use live regions.
Architect's suggestion / options: Recommendation: use whichever is more reliable with NVDA. If both work, keep ariaNotify.
PO Response: Go with area notify unless I report a problem.

Question: The Windows installer installs TobyMap for you only, in your own Programs folder, so it needs no administrator prompt. It is not signed, because signing costs money, so Windows SmartScreen may say it is unrecognised the first time: choose More info, then Run anyway. Is installing for the current user acceptable, and is the SmartScreen step acceptable for testers?
Why it matters: Installing for all users needs an administrator prompt. Signing would remove the SmartScreen warning but needs a paid certificate.
Architect's suggestion / options: Recommendation: install for the current user, unsigned, until there are outside users. Revisit signing before version 1.0.
PO Response: Agree with recommendation.  If needed, I can provide a wav file for the soft tick sound.

Question: The web version downloads about 17 MB the first time (Pyodide, which runs Python in the browser, plus NumPy and PyYAML), and takes about 9 to 10 seconds to start on this laptop in the automatic tests. Later visits should be quicker once the browser has cached it. Is that start-up time acceptable for the web version, while spike S4 looks at reducing it?
Why it matters: Python in the browser is what lets the web version share all its logic with the desktop (AD-1, AD-9). The cost is the start-up time.
Architect's suggestion / options: Recommendation: accept it for now; spike S4 measures it properly and looks at caching and a smaller download.
PO Response: Recommendation accepted.

Question: You asked for a key that takes focus to the map, as well as Ctrl+Alt+M for the menu bar in the web version. I suggest Ctrl+Alt+G (G for globe), in both the desktop and web versions, from any region. It would say the place under the centre, as arriving on the map by Tab does. Ctrl+Alt+M and Ctrl+Alt+G are not NVDA keys, but some keyboard layouts use Ctrl+Alt for accented letters. Is Ctrl+Alt+G acceptable, or would you prefer another key?
Why it matters: From the Information panel or Details, the map is now one or two Tab presses away. A key makes it one press from anywhere.
Architect's suggestion / options: Ctrl+Alt+G, in both versions.

Question: You ruled out eSpeak NG, and asked that the desktop and web versions do not use different voices (DP90). So the web version needs Piper in the browser too, with the Alba voice. That adds about 60 MB to the first download, on top of about 17 MB for Pyodide. Later visits use the browser's cached copy. Is that acceptable? The alternative is a smaller, lower-quality Piper voice for the web, of about 20 MB, if one with a clear licence exists.
Why it matters: It decides what spike S4 has to fit into the web start-up.
Architect's suggestion / options: Accept the 60 MB, but load the voice after the map is ready, so TobyMap can be used while the voice downloads.
